fetched_contents.text: [99mTc]Tilmanocept Accurately Detects Sentinel Lymph Nodes and Predicts Node Pathology Status in Patients with Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Head and Neck: Results of a Phase III Multi-institutional Trial Abstract Background [99mTc]Tilmanocept, a novel CD206 receptor-targeted radiopharmaceutical, was evaluated in an open-label, phase III trial to determine the false negative rate (FNR) of sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) relative to the pathologic nodal status in patients with intraoral or cutaneous head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) undergoing tumor resection, SLNB, and planned elective neck dissection (END). Negative predictive value (NPV), overall accuracy of SLNB, and the impact of radiopharmaceutical injection timing relative to surgery were assessed. Methods and Findings This multicenter, non-randomized, single-arm trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT00911326) enrolled 101 patients with T1–T4, N0, and M0 HNSCC. Patients received 50 µg [99mTc]tilmanocept radiolabeled with either 0.5 mCi (same day) or 2.0 mCi (next day), followed by lymphoscintigraphy, SLNB, and END. All excised tissues were evaluated for tissue type and tumor presence. [99mTc]Tilmanocept identified one or more SLNs in 81 of 83 patients (97.6 %). Of 39 patients identified with any tumor-positive nodes (SLN or non-SLN), one patient had a single tumor-positive non-SLN in whom all SLNs were tumor-negative, yielding an FNR of 2.56 %; NPV was 97.8 % and overall accuracy was 98.8 %. No significant differences were observed between same-day and next-day procedures. Conclusions Use of receptor-targeted [99mTc]tilmanocept for lymphatic mapping allows for a high rate of SLN identification in patients with intraoral and cutaneous HNSCC. SLNB employing [99mTc]tilmanocept accurately predicts the pathologic nodal status of intraoral HNSCC patients with low FNR, high NPV, and high overall accuracy. The use of [99mTc]tilmanocept for SLNB in select patients may be appropriate and may obviate the need to perform more extensive procedures such as END. ---------------------------------------- Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) of both mucosal and cutaneous origin carries variable propensity to metastasize to regional cervical nodes. The presence of nodal metastases is the most important negative prognostic factor for long-term survival.1–3 Thus, accurate identification and treatment of lymphatic metastases is important for this patient population. As current methods, including physical examination and radiologic imaging, lack sufficient sensitivity and specificity,4,5 elective neck dissection (END) has been the gold standard for assessing the presence or absence of lymphatic disease in patients without overt clinical or radiographic nodal metastases (cN0) undergoing surgical management of HNSCC.6 However, END is associated with significant potential morbidity, including pain, contour changes, shoulder dysfunction, and lip paresis, as well as negative impact upon quality of life.7–9 Furthermore, it may be argued that END is unnecessary in a large proportion of patients; for example, 70–80 % of patients initially presenting with early-stage oral cavity carcinoma (T1 or T2, cN0) ultimately prove to be free of lymphatic metastases.8,10–12 Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) has been advocated as a less invasive means of achieving accurate diagnostic assessment of regional metastatic tumor potential while reducing morbidity compared with more extensive procedures.9 Several studies have examined SLNB in HNSCC using radiolabeled colloid.13–18 Despite excellent negative predictive values (NPV), the false negative rate (FNR) of SLNB for HNSCC (i.e. percentage of cases with overall positive END, SLN pathology-negative) appears variable and reached nearly 10 % in the two largest multicenter series.14,18 Characteristics of radiolabeled colloid, including its particulate nature and lack of specific binding, may in part contribute to observed FNR when used for SLNB in HNSCC. [99mTc]Tilmanocept, approved by the US FDA and recently granted marketing authorization by the European Medicine Agency’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use for breast cancer, melanoma, and oral HNSCC SLN detection, is a novel, receptor-targeted, non-particulate radiopharmaceutical that consists of multiple diethylenetriaminepentaacetic acid (DTPA) molecules for 99mTc chelation and mannose moieties for CD206 receptor binding tethered to a dextran scaffold. The small molecular size (7 nm diameter) of tilmanocept and its specific targeting to CD206 mannose-binding receptors located on reticuloendothelial cells within lymph nodes permit rapid injection site clearance and avid, stable binding within target nodes.19 This article describes the results of an open-label, FDA-designated, phase III trial to assess the accuracy of [99mTc]tilmanocept used in conjunction with lymphoscintigraphy and SLNB to detect SLNs, as well as predict pathologic nodal status (i.e. presence vs. absence of metastatic disease) in patients with oral or cutaneous HNSCC undergoing SLNB and END. Methods Participants and Institutional Review/Consent Eligibility criteria included T1–T4a, cN0, and M0 HNSCC located in the oral cavity or cutaneous head and neck region. Clinical nodal staging was confirmed by negative results from contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan, gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), or neck ultrasound. Patients with a history of neck dissection, gross injury to the neck, or radiotherapy to the neck or receiving systemic cytotoxic therapy were excluded from the trial. Subject enrollment occurred across 13 centers. The protocol and informed consent were approved by the Institutional Review Boards of each center, and the study met all applicable regulatory and ethical requirements. fetched_contents.text: Detection of melanoma, breast cancer and head and neck squamous cell cancer sentinel lymph nodes by Tc-99m Tilmanocept (Lymphoseek®) Abstract Technetium-99m-labeled Tilmanocept or Lymphoseek® (Cardinal Health, Dublin, Ohio) is a soluble, synthetic molecule with a small diameter (7 nm), which is comprised of technetium-99m chelated to a dextran backbone containing multiple units of mannose ligands with a high affinity for CD206, a receptor located on the surface of macrophages and dendritic cells that are found in high concentration in lymph nodes. It enables quick transit from the injection site and rapid lymph node accumulation. The binding of mannose ligand and CD206 results in the internalization of the ligand and receptor into the cell. Once the Technetium-99m-labeled Tilmanocept (Lymphoseek®) reaches the lymph node, it is readily internalized by the macrophages and dendritic cells within the draining lymph nodes. Technetium-99m-labeled Tilmanocept (Lymphoseek®) has been extensively studied as a radioisotope for detection of sentinel lymph nodes in melanoma, breast cancer and head and neck squamous cell carcinoma in clinical trials. Based on its safety and ability to detect sentinel lymph nodes satisfactorily, it has been approved by the FDA to use as a radioisotope for preoperative lymphoscintigraphy for identification of sentinel lymph nodes in these types of cancer. Further, the FDA has expanded approval of Technetium-99m-labeled for sentinel lymph node mapping of all solid tumors as well as in pediatric patients. Keywords: Tc-99m-labeled Tilmanocept, Lymphoseek®, Sentinel lymph nodes, Melanoma, Breast cancer, Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma Introduction The concept of sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) to stage the regional lymph node with avoidance of a traditional radical lymph node dissection has been developed by the work of two SLN surgical pioneers, Cabanas [1] with the penile carcinoma model based on the anatomical location of SLNs and Morton [2] with the melanoma model based on the lymphatic drainage of the primary site to the SLNs. Subsequent clinical trials in melanoma [3] and breast cancer [4] have firmly established that SLNB is a reliable staging procedure for the regional nodal basin. The significance of the SLN concept is that a radical lymph node dissection with increased morbidity can be spared if the SLNB is negative. Although blue dye or isosulfan blue (Lymphazurin™) was used in the original study for melanoma SLN procedure [2], the critical development was the adoption of radiotracer [5, 6] to identify SLNs. Technetium-99m sulfur colloid was widely used as it serves two major goals: (1) the ability to define the drainage patterns of the primary cancer site such as melanoma [6] or breast cancer to the regional nodal basin preoperatively and (2) facilitation of intraoperative identification of SLNs using a gamma probe [5]. Preoperative lymphoscintigraphy is mandatory for determining the SLN basin(s) for primary melanoma as it may arise from any site of the body. Singular or multiple nodal basins may be detected. For example, a primary melanoma in the distal lower extremity, it may drain to the popliteal basin, in addition to the inguinal basin. A lesion in the upper extremity, it may drain to the epitrochlear basin, in addition to the axillary basin. A truncal primary melanoma may drain to multiple sites including the lower neck, bilateral axillae and groins. On the other hand, a primary breast cancer usually drains to the ipsilateral axilla. It is mandatory to have preoperative lymphoscintigraphy to map out the exact locations of the nodal basins draining the primary melanoma site. Figure 1 shows the various patterns of lymphatic drainage from melanoma of different anatomic sites to different nodal basin. In the 1990s, when SLNB was being developed, both Lymphazurin™ and radiotracer were used as the blue dye added the visualization of the SLN being blue. The identification of sentinel nodes was reported to be increased to 97% to 99% [7, 8]. To date, radiotracer such as Tc-99m sulfur colloid is used to identify the SLN basins by lymphoscintigraphy and to detect the SLNs by a gamma probe intraoperatively and when used alone, successful mapping of SLNs may result in localization over 95–98% [9, 10]. In this review article, the identification of SLNs in melanoma, breast cancer and head and neck cancer using Technetium-99m-labeled Tilmanocept (Lymphoseek®) will be discussed in detail. The content of this review is based on the presentations by Stanley Leong on the identification of melanoma and breast cancer SLNs and by Stephen Lai on the identification of head and neck cancer SLNs using Lymphoseek during a mini-symposium being sponsored by Cardinal Health (Dublin, OH). Characteristics of Technetium-99m-labeled Tilmanocept We and others have studied a novel radiotracer, Technetium-99m-labeled Tilmanocept (Lymphoseek®), to identify SLNs [11, 12]. Technetium-99m-labeled Tilmanocept (Lymphoseek®) is a soluble, synthetic molecule with a small diameter (7 nm) that enables rapid transit from the injection site and rapid lymph node accumulation. The current evidence supports 99mTc-tilmanocept as a reasonably effective tracer for sentinel lymph node (SLN) identification in head and neck cancer, though the evidence base is narrower than for some other cancers and includes both phase III trial and comparative study evidence.

**Reported sensitivity and specificity across head and neck cancer subtypes**  
The phase III head and neck cancer trial reported that [99mTc]tilmanocept identified one or more SLNs in 81 of 83 patients (97.6%), and among 39 patients identified with any tumor-positive nodes (SLN or non-SLN), one patient had a single tumor-positive non-SLN in whom all SLNs were tumor-negative, yielding an FNR of 2.56% and an NPV of 97.8%. Overall accuracy was 98.8% [N1-F1]. The study explicitly focused on intraoral and cutaneous head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), indicating that the reported performance is specific to these subtypes rather than a broad HNSCC population [N1-F1]. The evidence does not provide separate specificity numbers for subtypes, but the overall high NPV and low FNR suggest strong specificity for detecting metastatic involvement when nodes are present [N1-F1].

**Clinical study design and sample size**  
The core evidence is a phase III, open-label, non-randomized, single-arm trial with 101 patients with T1–T4a, cN0, and M0 HNSCC [N1-F1]. Patients received 50 µg [99mTc]tilmanocept radiolabeled with either 0.5 mCi (same day) or 2.0 mCi (next day), followed by lymphoscintigraphy, SLNB, and planned elective neck dissection (END). The study was multicenter and enrolled across 13 centers, with institutional review and regulatory approval [N1-F1]. The sample size is relatively modest for a definitive diagnostic trial, and the single-arm design limits direct comparison against other tracers in this dataset [N1-F1].

**Impact on surgical decision-making and staging accuracy**  
The trial’s conclusions emphasize that SLNB using [99mTc]tilmanocept “accurately predicts the pathologic nodal status” of intraoral HNSCC patients and may obviate the need for more extensive procedures such as END [N1-F1]. This suggests that the tracer improves staging accuracy by reducing the proportion of patients who require END, which is important because END is associated with significant morbidity [N1-F1]. The study also states that the false-negative rate is low enough to support the use of SLNB in select patients [N1-F1]. In other evidence, a case-study-style source notes a false-negative rate of 2.6% for detecting patients with cancer-positive nodes and a negative predictive value of 97.8% [N3-R4]. Together, these sources indicate that 99mTc-tilmanocept improves staging accuracy and supports more selective surgery, but the evidence is still limited to head and neck cancer rather than broader cancer types [N3-R4].

**Evidence for false-negative cases and reasons for failure**  
The phase III trial reported one false-negative case among 39 patients identified with any tumor-positive nodes, yielding an FNR of 2.56% [N1-F1]. The source also notes that no significant differences were observed between same-day and next-day procedures [N1-F1]. A comparative study against sulfur colloid notes that the efficacy of tilmanocept in sentinel lymph-node mapping and identification in breast cancer was evaluated in a comparative review and meta-analysis [N2-R3], but that evidence is not directly about false-negative rates in head and neck cancer. A separate source states that in head and neck SCC, TL was reported to have a much lower false-negative rate than 99mTc-labeled colloid [N3-R5]. Another source describes a cost-effectiveness study that explicitly states that tilmanocept “allowed for improved SLNB success in the head and neck with lower false-negative rates compared with sulfur colloid” [N3-R3]. These sources collectively support the idea that false-negative failure is uncommon but still present, and that it may be less frequent than with colloid-based approaches [N1-F1][N3-R3][N3-R5]. The phase III trial also notes that the false-negative case occurred in a patient with a single tumor-positive non-SLN in whom all SLNs were tumor-negative, implying that the failure may have been due to the tumor-positive node draining outside the SLN set rather than a failure of tracer uptake [N1-F1].

Overall, the current evidence indicates that 99mTc-tilmanocept is effective for SLN identification in head and neck cancer, with strong accuracy and a low false-negative rate, especially in the phase III trial [N1-F1][N3-R4]. However, the evidence is still limited to HNSCC subtypes and is mainly derived from one major trial rather than broad meta-analysis-level data across all subtypes [N1-F1][N3-R4].

The current evidence suggests that 99mTc-tilmanocept has favorable technical characteristics for sentinel lymph node mapping in head and neck cancer, but it is not without limitations, particularly in terms of false negatives and dependence on imaging protocol and anatomy.

**Imaging protocol and timing that optimize uptake and detection**  
The phase III head and neck trial used 50 µg [99mTc]tilmanocept radiolabeled with either 0.5 mCi (same day) or 2.0 mCi (next day), followed by lymphoscintigraphy, SLNB, and planned END [N1-F1]. The study found no significant differences between same-day and next-day procedures [N1-F1], suggesting that timing may not strongly affect detection in this cohort. A broader review article explains that tilmanocept is a soluble, synthetic molecule with a small diameter (7 nm) that enables rapid transit from the injection site and rapid lymph node accumulation [N4-F4]. It also states that the binding of mannose ligand and CD206 results in internalization of the ligand and receptor into the cell, and that once tilmanocept reaches the lymph node, it is readily internalized by macrophages and dendritic cells [N4-F4]. This suggests that optimal uptake and detection depend on rapid lymphatic transit and binding to CD206-positive reticuloendothelial cells in lymph nodes, rather than prolonged or delayed imaging protocols [N4-F4]. The trial also notes that the tracer was used in conjunction with lymphoscintigraphy and SLNB, indicating that imaging timing is integrated with preoperative and intraoperative workflow [N1-F1].

**Differences in accuracy by tumor site and lymphatic anatomy**  
The evidence is strongest for intraoral and cutaneous HNSCC, where the phase III trial reported high SLN identification and low FNR [N1-F1]. The same source emphasizes that HNSCC has variable propensity to metastasize to regional cervical nodes and that END is the gold standard for assessing lymphatic disease, but END is associated with significant morbidity [N1-F1]. The source also notes that the false-negative rate of SLNB for HNSCC can be variable, reaching nearly 10% in some multicenter series, and that the particulate nature and lack of specific binding of radiolabeled colloid may contribute to FNR [N1-F1]. This implies that anatomical variation in lymphatic drainage and tumor location may affect accuracy, but the evidence here is specific to HNSCC rather than general lymphatic anatomy [N1-F1]. The comparative study evidence against sulfur colloid suggests that tilmanocept may perform better in head and neck SCC than colloid, but the exact site-specific differences are not quantified in the provided excerpts [N3-R3][N3-R5].

**Limitations such as false negatives, cold tracers, and imaging artifacts**  
The phase III trial reported an FNR of 2.56% and NPV of 97.8% [N1-F1]. A case-study-style source reports a false-negative rate of 2.6% for detecting patients with cancer-positive nodes [N3-R4]. These false-negative rates are low but still nonzero, and the trial notes that the false-negative case occurred in a patient with a single tumor-positive non-SLN in whom all SLNs were tumor-negative [N1-F1]. This suggests that false negatives may arise when the tumor-positive node drains outside the identified SLN set rather than from tracer failure itself. The evidence does not provide a direct “cold tracer” rate, but the general discussion of radiolabeled colloid notes that its particulate nature and lack of specific binding may contribute to FNR [N1-F1]. The review article also states that tilmanocept is receptor-targeted and non-particulate, which may explain why it may have lower false-negative rates than colloid [N4-F4]. Imaging artifacts are not specifically discussed in the provided excerpts, so this remains only implied by the broader discussion of uptake and detection rather than directly demonstrated [N4-F4].

**How performance compares to alternative tracers or blue dye**  
The comparative study against sulfur colloid indicates that tilmanocept was more effective than sulfur colloid in early stage oral cavity cancer, with a lower false-negative rate [N3-R3]. The same cost-effectiveness study states that tilmanocept was more effective than sulfur colloid by 0.12 QALYs and that it was more costly, but the overall ICER was under the threshold for cost-effectiveness [N3-F3]. A broader comparative review mentions a comparative review and meta-analysis of tilmanocept for sentinel lymph-node mapping and identification in breast cancer [N2-R3], but the provided excerpts do not give specific numbers for head and neck cancer. The melanoma/head and neck comparison source notes that tilmanocept detected a node in more patients than blue dye in one study, and that the difference was statistically significant [N4-R1]. Another source notes that combined phase III trials evaluating tilmanocept and blue dye showed that tilmanocept detected a node in more patients than blue dye [N4-R5]. These sources support the idea that tilmanocept may outperform blue dye in SLN detection, but the provided excerpts do not quantify how much better it is in head and neck cancer specifically [N4-R1][N4-R5].

Overall, the evidence indicates that 99mTc-tilmanocept has favorable technical properties for sentinel lymph node mapping in head and neck cancer, with rapid uptake, receptor targeting, and relatively low false-negative rates [N1-F1][N4-F4]. However, it is not perfect: false negatives can still occur, especially when the tumor drains outside the SLN set, and its performance may vary by tumor site and lymphatic anatomy [N1-F1][N3-R4]. Compared to alternative tracers, it appears to perform better than sulfur colloid and possibly better than blue dye in some settings, but the provided evidence is not fully quantitative for head and neck cancer alone [N3-R3][N4-R1][N4-R5].

**Reported adverse events and patient tolerability**  
The phase III head and neck trial reported 13 serious adverse events in the trial, though none were associated with Lymphoseek [N5-R2]. This is important because it suggests that the tracer itself did not cause the serious events, but it does not rule out other procedural factors. The excerpt does not provide detailed tolerability data beyond the serious event count, so the evidence is limited in depth [N5-R2]. The broader clinical-trials evidence also includes a nonrandomized phase III trial designed for head and neck squamous cell carcinomas [N5-R3], but the provided excerpt does not add specific adverse-event detail beyond the trial-level serious events [N5-R3]. Overall, the current evidence indicates a favorable tolerability profile, but it is not sufficiently detailed to fully characterize day-to-day patient reactions [N5-R2].

**Impact on surgical workflow and operating time**  
The phase III trial’s conclusion explicitly states that SLNB employing [99mTc]tilmanocept “accurately predicts the pathologic nodal status” and may obviate the need for more extensive procedures such as END [N1-F1]. This implies a workflow benefit: by identifying SLNs more reliably, the procedure can avoid unnecessary END and reduce the burden of more invasive surgery [N1-F1]. The trial also notes that patients received 50 µg of [99mTc]tilmanocept radiolabeled with either 0.5 mCi or 2.0 mCi, followed by lymphoscintigraphy, SLNB, and END [N1-F1]. The inclusion of lymphoscintigraphy and the planned END suggests that the tracer is integrated into a preoperative-to-intraoperative workflow rather than being used as a standalone intraoperative agent [N1-F1]. However, the provided excerpts do not directly quantify operating time or procedural efficiency, so the evidence is indirect [N1-F1].

**Radiation exposure and safety profile**  
The evidence is limited, but the trial provides enough detail to infer a reasonable safety profile. The tracer was radiolabeled with 0.5 mCi or 2.0 mCi, and the trial included 101 patients with HNSCC [N1-F1]. No serious adverse events were directly associated with Lymphoseek in the trial [N5-R2]. The broader discussion notes that the tracer is approved by the FDA and that it is a non-particulate, receptor-targeted radiopharmaceutical [N1-F1][N4-F4]. This suggests a radiation profile that is clinically acceptable for diagnostic use, but the excerpts do not provide specific radiation doses, effective doses, or comparisons with other tracers [N1-F1][N4-F4]. The evidence therefore supports a favorable safety profile, but it does not fully quantify radiation risk [N5-R2].

The evidence from the four upstream branches indicates that **99mTc-tilmanocept is a reasonably effective and accurate tracer for sentinel lymph node (SLN) mapping in head and neck cancer**, but the evidence base is still limited and not universally comprehensive across all subtypes and settings. The core evidence from the phase III head and neck cancer trial shows strong effectiveness. This is important because it suggests that the tracer is effective at identifying SLNs in a clinically relevant patient population and that timing may not strongly affect detection in this cohort [N1-F1].

The broader evidence further supports effectiveness. A case-study-style source reports a false-negative rate of 2.6% for detecting patients with cancer-positive nodes and a negative predictive value of 97.8% [N3-R4]. A comparative study against sulfur colloid notes that tilmanocept “allowed for improved SLNB success in the head and neck with lower false-negative rates compared with sulfur colloid” [N3-R3].
